entries.note: The root box is right on all three counts. Pokorny's lemma is 'eḱuo-s (*heḱuo-), Meaning: horse, Page(s): 301-302', so 'Indo-European Ekwos : horse, POK:301' reproduces his headword, gloss and page exactly; Watkins's appendix has 'ekwo-. Horse ... [Pok. ekuo-s 301.]'. Modern reconstruction writes it *h₁éḱwos (Wiktionary; Kapović would drop the laryngeal), traditionally explained as a derivative of *h₁oh₁ḱus 'swift', though Buck already warned that the 'root connection [is] wholly obscure'. The chart is a good one: the Iranian side (Av. aspa-, the long series of -aspa names, aspast/alfalfa, astar) and the Greek side (hippos, Philippos) are both genuine and are carried by good references — Moʿin's footnote on Borhān p.119 supplies the entire alfalfa chain in one sentence and AHD:32 supplies it again. Five corrections are needed, none of them touching the root: (1) aspa-bāra is Old Persian asa-bāra-, not Avestan; (2) Tahmāsb belongs to Av. taxma- 'brave', not to Pokorny's *Tūmāspa- 'having fat horses'; (3) Vīštāspa means 'having horses untied (for racing)' (Iranica) or, with Moʿin/Bartholomae, 'having spent horses' — 'gray' is unsupported; (4) Gošnāsp comes from Av. varəšni- 'male (ram)' as Horn says on the very page cited (HRN:206), not from aršan-; (5) Middle Persian astar is inherited from OP *asatara-, a cognate of Skt. aśvatara-, not a borrowing from Sanskrit. Two smaller points: the Avestan compound behind aspast is better reconstructed *aspa-sti- (AHD) and is not attested in the Avesta, and English alfalfa passed through Spanish. The two BQT:1819 citations on the aspa and aspa-asa boxes point to the گشتاسب page and belong to the Vīštāspa box instead.
entries.note_fa: خودِ ریشه از هر سه جهت درست است: پوکورنی مادهٔ eḱuo-s «اسب» را در صفحات ۳۰۱–۳۰۲ آورده و واتکینز در پیوست فرهنگ American Heritage همان را با ارجاع «Pok. ekuo-s 301» تکرار کرده است؛ بازسازی امروزی *h₁éḱwos است. نمودار در کل استوار است: هم شاخهٔ ایرانی (aspa اوستایی، زنجیرهٔ نام‌های -اسپ، اسپست/الفلفه، استر) و هم شاخهٔ یونانی (hippos، Philippos) اصیل‌اند و حاشیهٔ معین بر برهان قاطع (ص ۱۱۹) تمام زنجیرهٔ «اسپست ← سریانی ← فصفصه ← الفلفه» را در یک جمله می‌آورد. پنج تصحیح لازم است و هیچ‌یک به خودِ ریشه مربوط نیست: ۱) aspa-bāra پارسی باستان (asa-bāra-) است نه اوستایی؛ ۲) «تهماسب» از taxma- اوستایی «دلیر» است نه از *Tūmāspa- «دارندهٔ اسبان فربه»؛ ۳) معنای Vīštāspa «دارندهٔ اسبان رهاشده (برای مسابقه)» یا به گفتهٔ معین و بارتولمه «اسبان از کار افتاده» است و «خاکستری» پشتوانه ندارد؛ ۴) «گشناسپ» از varəšni- اوستایی است ــ همان‌گونه که هرن در صفحهٔ ۲۰۶ که نورایی به آن ارجاع داده می‌گوید ــ نه از aršan-؛ ۵) astar پهلوی موروثی است از *asatara- پارسی باستان و هم‌ریشهٔ aśvatara- سنسکریت، نه وام‌گرفته از آن. دو نکتهٔ کوچک‌تر: بازسازی بهترِ اصلِ «اسپست» *aspa-sti- است و در اوستا گواهی نشده، و alfalfa انگلیسی از راه اسپانیایی رفته است.

nodes.derivation: Av. aspa- 'horse' is the direct Iranian continuant of PIE *h₁éḱwos: the palatal *ḱ gives Proto-Iranian *ć, and the cluster *ćw yields Avestan/Median sp (Old Persian s), so *h₁eḱwo- > PIr. *Hácwah > Av. aspa-, OP asa-; Kent §90 states the rule verbatim ('pIE *eḱuo- "horse", OP asa- ... OP aspa- (with Med. sp) in Vistaspa-; Av. aspa-, Skt. aśva, Lt. equos'). Bartholomae's dictionary has aspa- and dozens of compounds in -aspa-. The second word is the weak point: the attested form is Old Persian asa-bāra- 'horseman' (DB 2.2 asabaraibiš), not an Avestan *aspa-bāra-; Avestan uses aspa- in compounds but the 'rider' word is Old Persian/Median, built on the byform asa- + -bāra- from PIE *bher- 'to carry' (Nourai's ☞Bher 1 is right). The literal sense is 'borne by a horse' rather than 'horse load'.
nodes.derivation_fa: اوستایی aspa- «اسب» بازماندهٔ مستقیم هندواروپایی آغازین *h₁éḱwos است: کام‌واکِ *ḱ در ایرانی به *ć بدل شده و خوشهٔ *ćw در اوستایی و مادی به sp و در پارسی باستان به s تبدیل شده است (aspa- در برابر asa-)؛ کِنت (بند ۹۰) همین قاعده را می‌آورد. امّا جزء دوم، «aspa-bāra»، در اوستا گواهی نشده؛ صورت گواهی‌شده پارسی باستان asa-bāra- «اسب‌سوار» است (سنگ‌نبشتهٔ بیستون) که از صورت فرعی asa- به علاوهٔ -bāra- از ریشهٔ *bher- «بردن» ساخته شده. پس ادعای نورایی دربارهٔ aspa درست است ولی برچسب زبانیِ aspa-bāra باید «پارسی باستان» می‌بود.

nodes.derivation: NP اسب asb continues MP asp unchanged but for the late orthographic/phonetic b for p (classical and Dari still asp; the spelling اسب is the modern Iranian norm, اسپ the older one). NP سوار savār is MP aswār with loss of the initial unstressed a- (aphaeresis) — Hübschmann §, 'mit Ausfall des p: suvār "Reiter" = ap. asabāra-', i.e. OP asabāra- > MP aswār > NP suwār/savār; the word is thus a doublet-free direct descendant, and the Persian phrase اسب‌سوار is a later recompounding. Wiktionary gives the same chain (اسب < MP asp < OP aspa/Median *aspah; سوار < MP ʾswbʾl aswār).

nodes.derivation: All four are possessive (bahuvrīhi) compounds whose second member is aspa-, so the arrow from the root is right; two of the four glosses are not what the sources say. (1) tum-āspa: Pokorny p.1082 under *teu- 'to swell; fat; strong' does list 'Avestan *tuma- in Tumaspana- from Tumaspa- (i.e. one whose horses are fat)', and Bartholomae has 'tumāspana- patr. Adj. "von Tumāspa stammend"' (Yt.13.131) — so the Avestan name is real, but its sense is 'having fat/plump horses', and Schmitt's Iranica survey lists *Tūmāspa- only through the patronymic Tūmāspāna-. (2) kərəsāspa- is confirmed: Iranica, 'Kərəsāspa- (no. 216) "Possessing slender horses"'. (3) vīštāspa- is confirmed as a word, but modern onomastics glosses it 'possessing horses untied (for racing)' (Iranica no. 379, an old Aryan horse-racing term, vi- + šta- from stā-); Moʿin (Borhān p.1819, after Bartholomae col.1467) reads 'دارندهٔ اسب از کار افتاده' = 'whose horses are spent', which is Nourai's 'old horses'; nobody supports 'gray'. (4) baēvarə- '10,000' is Avestan (Bartholomae, with baēvarə.patay-, baēvarə.spasan- etc.), but there is no Avestan headword baēvarə.aspa-; the compound bēwar-asp is a Middle Persian epithet of Dahāg, so the box's language label is one stage too early.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر چهار واژه ترکیب دارندگی (بهوریهی) با جزء دوم aspa هستند، پس پیوند آنها با ریشه درست است؛ ولی دو معنی نادرست است. پوکورنی (ص ۱۰۸۲، ذیل *teu- «آماسیدن، فربه، نیرومند») صورت اوستایی *Tūmāspa- را از راه نام پدرسالاری Tūmāspāna- می‌آورد و آن را «دارندهٔ اسبان فربه» معنی می‌کند؛ بارتولمه هم tumāspana- را دارد. Kərəsāspa- «دارندهٔ اسبان لاغر» است (ایرانیکا). امّا Vīštāspa- را ریشه‌شناسی امروزی «دارندهٔ اسبان رهاشده (برای مسابقه)» می‌داند و معین در حاشیهٔ برهان (ص ۱۸۱۹، به پیروی بارتولمه ستون ۱۴۶۷) «دارندهٔ اسب از کار افتاده» می‌آورد؛ معنی «خاکستری» هیچ پشتوانه‌ای ندارد. سرانجام baēvarə «ده‌هزار» اوستایی است ولی ترکیب baēvarə.aspa- در فرهنگ بارتولمه نیامده و «بیوراسپ» لقب پهلوی ضحّاک است، نه واژه‌ای اوستایی.

nodes.derivation: Three of the four are textbook: Garšāsp < MP Kirsāsp < Av. Kərəsāspa- 'having slender horses' (Iranica no. 216; the Av. cluster rəs > NP rš/rs and final -a is lost); Goštāsp < MP Guštāsp < OP Vištāspa (itself the Median/Avestan Vīštāspa-), Wiktionary s.v. گشتاسپ giving exactly 'MP gwštsp < OP vi-š-t-a-s-p < Av. vištāspa', with the regular NP shift wi- > gu- (as in wišān > گشن, Av. vəhrka- > گرگ); Bīvarasp is the epithet of Żaḥḥāk/Dahāg, MP Dahāg ī bēwarasp 'having 10,000 horses', bēwar 'myriad' being Nyberg's 'bēvar [bywl] ten thousand'. The first name is the problem: Tahmāsb is standardly Av. Taxma-aspa- 'having brave/strong horses' (Av. taxma- 'brave, courageous', Iranica no. 304; MP Tahmāsp with xm > hm), not Pokorny's *Tūmāspa- 'having fat horses', which survives only in the patronymic Tūmāspāna- and is not continued in Persian. Nourai has crossed two homophonous-looking Avestan names.

nodes.derivation: Two of the four are exactly right, one is unattested and one is glossed on a guess. aurvaṱ.aspa- is in Bartholomae as '• j. ʼaurvataspa- Adj. "der schnelle Rosse hat"', used of the sun (hvarə.xšaēta- ... aurvaṱ.aspəm, Yt.6.1) and as the name of Vīštāspa's father — Nourai's '(with) swift horses' is verbatim right. arəǰaṱ.aspa- is likewise in Bartholomae, '• j. arəǰaṱ.aspa- m. EN. eines Hyaona-Fürsten' (Yt.9.30, 5.109), from arəj- 'to be worth', so '(with) valuable horses' is the standard analysis (Iranica s.v. ARJĀSP). Jāmāspa- is a real Avestan name (Bartholomae s.v., with the patronymic Jāmāspana-), but the first element is admittedly obscure: proposals are Vedic kṣāmá- 'singed', Gershevitch's 'leading horses' and Schwartz's 'he who bridles horses'; 'owning horses' is nobody's. Finally *aršan-aspa- is not in Bartholomae at all: aršan- 'male, stallion' is well attested on its own, and compound names like auruša.aspa- 'having white horses' show the type, but this particular compound has to be reconstructed.

nodes.derivation: Lohrāsb, Arjāsp and Jāmāsb are straightforward continuants of the Avestan names of the parent box: Auruuaṱ.aspa- > MP Lohrāsp (Av. aurvaṱ- > MP lohr- with the familiar r-metathesis/dissimilation of the Šāh-nāma onomastics) — he is Goštāsp's father in the epic; Arəǰaṱ.aspa- > MP/NP Arjāsp, the Xyōn king (Iranica); Jāmāspa- > MP Jāmāsp, Vīštāspa's minister, the -b of جاماسب being the same late spelling as in اسب. Gošnāsp, however, does not belong under aršan-aspa: NP/MP gušn 'male, stallion' comes from Av. varəšni- / PIr. *wr̥šni- with the regular Persian change of initial *w- before a rounded vowel to g- (exactly as Av. vəhrka- > گرگ gorg), and Horn, on the very page Nourai cites (no.925, p.206), spells this out and names Gušnasp as the example. Aršāsp itself is a Šāh-nāma-tradition name best derived from *Aršan-aspa-, but neither the Avestan compound nor the Persian name could be documented in an accessible reference (Moʿin's vol.5, which Nourai cites, is not available).

nodes.derivation: The Aramaic/Syriac stage is certain, the exact form less so. Syriac/Jewish Aramaic has ʾaspastā / ʾaspestā 'lucerne' (Wiktionary s.v. فصفص: 'Borrowed from Aramaic אַסְפַּסְתָּא (ʾaspastā) / ܐܰܣܦܷܣܬܳܐ (ʾaspestā, "lucerne"), from Akkadian aspastu, from Old Median *aspāstiš'), i.e. with initial a-, not p-. AHD explains the p-form as Coptic: Arabic fiṣfiṣa comes 'probably via Coptic p-espesta: p-, masculine sing. definite article + espesta, alfalfa, from Aramaic espestā, from Middle Persian aspast'. So the pespesta Nourai puts in a Syriac box is the form that mediated to Arabic, but its p- is most likely the Coptic article agglutinated to the Aramaic word, and the borrowing route Pahlavi > Aramaic/Syriac > Arabic is exactly what Moʿin states on Borhān p.119.

nodes.derivation: Sanskrit अश्वतर aśvatara- is a real word and does belong to *h₁éḱwos: it is aśva- 'horse' plus the contrastive/comparative suffix -tara- (as in Lat. dexter, Gk. -teros), literally 'the more horse-like one' — but its lexical meaning is 'mule', not the vague 'related to a horse' of the chart, which is Moʿin's paraphrase (Moʿin s.v. استر: '[= ستر؛ مربوط به اسب، قس. قاطر] (جان.) قاطر'). Horn no.86 cites 'ai. aśvatará- "Maulesel"'. The formation is old and shared: the same suffix on the same noun gives Old Persian *asatara- and Middle Persian astar, so aśvatara- is best regarded as the Indic member of an Indo-Iranian pair, not as a source (see node #16).
nodes.derivation_fa: سنسکریت aśvatara- واژه‌ای واقعی و از همین ریشه است: aśva- «اسب» به‌علاوهٔ پسوند برتری/تقابل -tara-، تحت‌اللفظ «آنکه بیشتر اسب‌گونه است»؛ امّا معنای فرهنگ‌نامه‌ای آن «استر/قاطر» است نه «مربوط به اسب» که تعبیر معین است (معین ذیل «استر»: «[= ستر؛ مربوط به اسب، قس. قاطر] (جان.) قاطر»). هرن (شمارهٔ ۸۶) نیز «ai. aśvatará- "استر"» می‌آورد. این ساخت هندوایرانی مشترک است و همان پسوند بر همان اسم، *asatara- پارسی باستان و astar پهلوی را داده است.

nodes.derivation: The empty box stands for Middle Persian astar 'mule', and the arrow drawn into it — Sanskrit aśvatara- > Pahlavi — is the wrong direction of transmission. Hübschmann derives the Persian word from an Old Persian *asatara- built on the byform asa- (with the same loss of p as in suvār < asabāra-) and treats Skt. aśvatara- as its cognate, not its source: 'mit Ausfall des p: suvār "Reiter" = ap. asabāra-; astar "Maulesel" = ap. *asatara-, skr. aśvatara-'. Wiktionary agrees: NP استر is 'inherited from Middle Persian ʾstl /astar/, from Old Persian *asatarah, from Proto-Iranian *Hacwatarāh, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Haćwatarás'. There is no evidence of a Sanskrit loan into Middle Persian here; the chart's Pahlavi box should hang directly from the root.

nodes.derivation: NP استر astar/ester 'mule' continues MP astar without change beyond the New Persian vowel notation; Horn no.86 lists 'ester "Maulesel": phlv. astar; ai. aśvatará-' with the Kurdish and Balochi cognates istir/histir, istal. nodes.derivation: Gk. ἵππος híppos 'horse' is the Greek reflex of *h₁éḱwos, via Proto-Hellenic *íkkʷos (Mycenaean i-qo); as Pokorny and Wiktionary both stress, the word is phonetically irregular — the expected form would be **épos, and the ι for ε, the rough breathing and the geminate -ππ- are unexplained (Kretschmer and Pokorny suspect an Illyrian/other IE dialect loan; the dialectal ἴκκος of Tarentum and Epidaurus points the same way). φίλιππος phílippos 'fond of horses' is a regular Greek possessive compound of φίλος 'dear, loving' + ἵππος, used from the classical period as an adjective and as the personal name Φίλιππος; Nourai's ☞Bhili cross-reference to the root of φίλος is right.
nodes.derivation_fa: یونانی ἵππος «اسب» بازتاب *h₁éḱwos است از راه هلنیِ آغازین *íkkʷos (میسنی i-qo)؛ چنانکه پوکورنی و ویکی‌واژه هر دو تأکید می‌کنند این صورت از نظر آوایی بی‌قاعده است: صورت مورد انتظار **épos بوده و ι به‌جای ε، دمِ درشت (rough breathing) و دوگانگیِ -ππ- توضیح‌ناپذیر است (کرچمر و پوکورنی وام‌گیری از گویشی ایلیریایی را محتمل می‌دانند؛ گونهٔ گویشی ἴκκος نیز همین را نشان می‌دهد). φίλιππος «اسب‌دوست» ترکیبی قاعده‌مند از φίλος «دوست‌دارنده» و ἵππος است که از دورهٔ کلاسیک هم صفت و هم نام خاص (Φίλιππος) بوده است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

nodes.derivation: The empty Latin box is the transmission stage for the two Greek words: Latin Philippus (the Macedonian king's name, then a Christian name through the apostle) and Late Latin hippopotamus, taken from Greek ἱπποπόταμος, itself an irregular univerbation of ὁ ἵππος ποτάμιος 'the horse of the river'. Latin's own inherited reflex of the root is equus, which the chart does not draw here. So the box is right as a route (Greek > Latin > French/English) but it holds borrowings, not an inherited Latin form.

nodes.derivation: The empty French box stands for Philippe, the French form of Latin Philippus (Old French Philippe, with the Latin -us dropped and the stress-final syllable reduced), the name of six kings of France and hence a standard European Christian name. It is the immediate model for the modern Persian transcription in the next box. No French word from this root reaches English on this chart, so the box's only function is the route Latin > French > Persian.

nodes.derivation: فیلیپ Filip is a modern Persian transcription of the European name, taken through French Philippe (whence the final -p and the long ī of the second syllable, against English 'Philip' with reduced vowel); Persian renders French /f/ with ف and both vowels with ی, the usual pattern for 19th-20th c. French borrowings (compare فیلسوف, فرانسه). Its ultimate sense 'horse lover' is the Greek φίλιππος, so the box is right; it is a learned borrowing, not a Persian inheritance from the root — a fact the chart shows correctly by hanging it from French rather than from the Iranian branch.

nodes.derivation: Both English words come through Latin from Greek, exactly as drawn. hippopotamus is attested in English from the 1560s, from Late Latin hippopotamus < Gk. ἱπποπόταμος; it displaced Middle English ypotame (c.1300), which reached English through Old French from the same Greek word, and Old English had glossed the animal sǣhengest 'sea-horse'. Philip is Latin Philippus < Gk. Φίλιππος; Watkins's appendix lists both HIPPOPOTAMUS and PHILIP among the English descendants of ekwo-.
